Reinforcement. Any consequence that increases the likelihood of a behavior being repeated.

B.F. Skinner distinguished between positive reinforcement, adding something desirable like food or praise, and negative reinforcement, removing something aversive like pain or discomfort. Positive reinforcement strengthens behavior by adding a desirable consequence. A rat gets food for pressing a lever, and a student gets praise for answering correctly. Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing or avoiding an aversive stimulus. A driver buckles a seatbelt to stop the alarm from beeping, and an animal escapes an electric shock by performing the desired action.

Crucially, both types increase behavior. They are distinct from punishment, which decreases behavior regardless of whether something is added or removed. The strength and pattern of reinforcement matters. Continuous reinforcement, rewarding every time, produces rapid learning but quick extinction when reinforcement stops. Intermittent schedules produce slower learning but greater persistence.

Variable-ratio schedules, rewarding after a random number of behaviors, are especially powerful. They create the gambling effect, where unpredictability sustains effort indefinitely. Reinforcement is species-universal. The same principle works on pigeons, rats, dogs, humans, and most creatures capable of learning, suggesting it reflects a fundamental property of nervous systems. The concept underpins applied behavior analysis, animal training, education, workplace motivation systems, and even video game design, which deliberately exploits reinforcement schedules to create compulsive engagement.

Reinforcement must be immediate, or very soon after the behavior, to be effective. Delayed reinforcement loses its power, which is why instant feedback loops in games and apps are so potent at shaping behavior and addiction. Satiation, the repetition of reinforcement until it no longer motivates, can reduce a reinforcer's power, while deprivation, removing access to the reinforcer, restores its strength.
